title: A single Tuvan throat singer can sing two notes at the same time
body: In khoomei, the throat singing of Tuva and Mongolia, a singer hums one low drone and at the same time shapes the mouth, tongue, lips and throat so that a single **overtone** of that drone rings out loudly enough to be heard as a second, whistling melody. Every voice contains those overtones, at whole-number multiples of the drone’s frequency; the trick is to filter out all but one, much as you shape vowels, only far more precisely. Melodies usually use the 6th to 13th partials, so a drone on C gives overtones from G to A, two to three octaves up.

slides.alt: A bar chart of a sung drone’s harmonics, numbered 1 to 13, with heights shrinking as the number rises. The eighth bar is tall and highlighted: the overtone the singer’s mouth amplifies into a second note.
slides.caption: Shaping the mouth boosts one harmonic until it sounds like a separate note.

slides.heading: Three main styles
items: Khoomei: softer; two or three harmonics audible above a mid drone
Sygyt: ‘whistling’, with strong, piercing, flute-like harmonics
Kargyraa: deep and growling, with an undertone an octave below

slides.heading: Imitating the land
slides.text: Sub-styles mimic the world around: borbangnadyr is a trill reminiscent of birds and travelling brooks, made with rapid movements of the tongue and lips, and ezenggileer pulses like the rhythm of riding a horse, by opening and closing the velum.

slides.question: How does a throat singer make one overtone stand out?
options: Shaping the mouth, like a vowel
slides.explanation: The mouth cavity is shaped, as when forming vowels, to select particular harmonics; in sygyt the tongue seals against the gums and the sound leaves through a small opening.
